# Ref Commons Playbook

When I start the game, I'll identify the total number of seasons and calculate my target total catch by multiplying the sustainable per-boat share by the number of seasons and the number of boats.

When I'm shown the current stock and sustainable share, I'll treat the sustainable share as my baseline catch for that season, not as a minimum I should exceed.

When I'm tempted to catch above the sustainable share because "other boats are doing it," I'll remember that this reasoning led me to a score of 60 when cooperation could have yielded higher returns. I'll stick to the sustainable amount unless I have clear evidence that others have defected systematically.

When I reach the final season, I'll catch at the sustainable level, not maximize. The final season is not my last opportunity to establish reputation or signal cooperation—it's just another season. Defecting on the last round only works if others are defecting too, and if they're not, I've just damaged the joint outcome for no real benefit.

When the stock begins to decline across seasons despite my sustainable catches, I'll assume that other players are slightly overfishing and I should maintain my sustainable catch rather than match their behavior. My job is to be predictably cooperative, not to race to the bottom.

I will not justify marginal increases above the sustainable share by saying "I'll catch 10 instead of 9.3 because boat 2 caught 10.5." That marginal thinking adds up across boats and seasons and destabilizes the fishery.

When calculating my catch each season, I'll submit the sustainable share rounded to one decimal place, not a figure I've adjusted upward based on my mood or performance so far.

# Playbook for ref_commons

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I recognize this as a commons dilemma where cooperation maximizes total catch but invites exploitation.

When I decide my opening catch, I will take moderately above the sustainable share—around 1.8-2x the stated sustainable amount—rather than the extreme I attempted before. This signals I won't be a pushover while preserving enough stock to avoid catastrophic collapse. Taking 20 when sustainable was 11.1 created a poor negotiating position.

When I observe other boats' catches in the feedback, I will treat them as signals of the local competition level, not as justification for immediate escalation. The pattern showed boats 2 and 3 converged toward sustainability; I should calibrate to match rather than race to the bottom.

When I am in mid-game seasons (not the first or last), I will catch very close to the sustainable share. My catches of 9.6 per season maintained stock health while securing a solid cumulative total. This is the equilibrium strategy that works.

When I reach the final season, I should not dramatically shift my strategy. End-game bonus captures are tempting but I finished poorly relative to modest, consistent catches. I will take the sustainable amount in the final season as I did in middle seasons.

When the stock visibly declines across my sessions, I will not interpret this as permission to overfish more. The stock fell from 87.1 to 83.6 over seasons 4-6 because boats 2 and 3 were gradually taking more. I should have recognized this and held discipline rather than creeping my catch upward.

I will not assume other boats will remain cooperative just because they started that way. Once I saw boat 1 (myself) take 20 in season 1, I should have expected the others to test boundaries too.

When tempted to squeeze extra catch in any season, I will remember: a final score of 68.7 came from taking sustainable amounts most of the time, not from occasional aggressive plays.

# Fishery Playbook

When I see the sustainable share calculation, I will treat it as a genuine baseline, not just a theoretical benchmark. Sustainable fishing across all seasons appears to produce stable stock and reliable catches.

When I'm tempted to exceed the sustainable share because "others might," I will remember that the evidence shows boats fishing at or near sustainable levels actually maintains the stock for future rounds. Each extra fish I take now directly reduces what I can catch later.

When I catch above the sustainable share early on, I will not compound the mistake by continuing to overcatch. I will return to sustainable levels immediately to prevent stock collapse.

When it's not the final season, I will never prioritize a marginal gain this round over the guaranteed larger gains from maintaining a healthy stock for remaining seasons.

When I'm ahead in cumulative catch, I will recognize this as a signal to fish at sustainable levels, not to accelerate my advantage. Being ahead means I can afford restraint.

When it's the final season and the sustainable share is presented, I will still respect it. The one-season advantage from overfishing is minimal and the game has shown that moderate discipline across all six seasons outperforms aggressive endgame strategies.

When I calculate my potential final score, I will not assume other boats will abandon sustainability in the final round just because it's the last round. They may show the same restraint they showed throughout.

My target is to catch at or very slightly above the sustainable share every single season, adjusting upward only if I see clear evidence that all boats are consistently exceeding it without consequence to total stock.
